utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecution versus Prlic et al. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Today on Tuesday, the 3rd of April, 2007, I'd like to greet everyone present in the courtroom, the Prosecution, Defence counsel, the accused, the Ambassador, and everyone else. The Trial Chamber now has an oral decision to render that concerns the Prosecution motion to have admitted into evidence Mr. Prlic's written statement. The Trial Chamber has decided that the motion must be filed confidentially, and secondly, subject to agreement among the parties, we plan to have a hearing on Thursday at 10.00 in the morning as the courtroom will be available at that time. This will be at the end of the witnesses examination. We will then have an hour's a break at noon so that everyone can have lunch, and we will then continue with our hearing so that the accused may have the opportunity to take the floor, as this is what they had requested. So this is what we would suggest to the parties concerned. I have also been informed that the Prosecution would like to add certain annexes to the conference held in Geneva. Mr. Scott, there's something you wanted to say. The document concerned is 9852.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Good afternoon to you, Mr. President, and to Your Honours, and to everyone in the courtroom. Yes, Your Honour. I provided notice to counsel and to the Chamber this morning that, in looking at the documents last night, I had been under the impression and I think again it was just -- admittedly with this much paper in the case it's sometimes difficult to keep it all straight, our Exhibit P 00116 that we used yesterday contained the full set of materials containing the Vance-Owen Peace Plan proposals as presented to the parties in early January 1993. When we ended the day yesterday and as I looked further at the documents last night, I noticed that it didn't -- it was not in fact the entire set of documents, whereas what has now been marked as P 09852, which is nothing more than a complete copy of UN Security Council document S/25050, which is available on the UN's web site, is a complete record of the proposals as they existed at that time, and I would ask for the Court's leave to work with that document in lieu of or in addition to the document we used yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I don't believe there will be any objections from the Defence. Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I don't believe so, Your Honour. At least not from Prlic, and I think I can speak for the rest of the Defence teams.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Scott, please continue with your examination-in-chief now.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I do appreciate counsel's accommodation on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, I'd like to pick up where we left off yesterday and back up just a little bit because we were at a bit of a disadvantage with some of the documentation yesterday afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I might also note, Your Honour, I meant to say that in terms of the diary, it appears that all the pages were in fact in the various bundles, but in some of the bundles they had been -- they had been misplaced. They were not in the right order, and I hope that's all been corrected at this point, and I apologise to both the Ambassador and to the Court and others for any confusion that was caused. I hope we'll do better today. I would ask that the usher please provide the witness with a copy of the exhibit we were just talking about, which is P 09852. I think that will be all right, usher. I think he'll be able to follow through all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Ambassador, this is the -- as you just heard me explain to the Court, this is a -- I believe, and we submit, the full packet of Vance-Owen Peace Plan propose -- material as it was presented to the three principal parties, the Croats, Muslims, and Serbs, on approximately -- between the 2nd and the 4th of January, 1993. Just to orient everyone in the courtroom because it is a rather fairly important document, can you just look at that document enough to say that you do recognise that as the set of Vance-Owen materials at that time?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Scott. This is the materials at that time, but it is not the final form of the Vance-Owen Peace Plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which, as everybody knows, I believe, was altered, understandably - that's what negotiations are all about - was altered after the initial presentation in early January.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And in fact, yes, indeed later this afternoon we will hopefully come to the version as it existed and was approved by at least two of the parties at the end of March 1993. The document sets out and those in the courtroom can look at it, a bit of history. This is actually the Secretary-General of the United Nations passing on his report about these developments to the Security Council on the 6th of January, 1993. There's a brief history of the talks and what was involved, the working groups, and how the process had worked up until to that point in time. Let me ask you to go to the pages -- the actual pages in this document are numbered in the upper part of the document, on the top part of each page, pages 1 through -- I believe the last page is 30 -- 36. So it's fairly easy to work with, I hope. Can I ask you to go to page 11 of the overall document, which is Annex III, the opening statement of Lord Owen. In the second paragraph, sir, of the Annex III it says: "As to the maps which you should now all have in front of you, there are 10 suggested provinces. We have ought to arbitrate on many conflicting claims and we have been very conscious of the need to follow the criteria that we established on 27 October. Boundaries of provinces to be drawn so as to constitute areas as geographically coherent as possible, taking into account ethnic, geographical (i.e., natural features such as rivers), historical, communications ... economic viability and other relevant factors." And Lord Owen goes on to say: "We have had to choose between conflicting claims and we cannot stress enough how vital it is that everyone accepts that there cannot be agreement without compromise, sometimes painful compromise." In looking -- before we go to the map, we just touch it -- briefly on -- because it will be shown on the map I wanted to ask you again, among the proposed provinces at that time, did the Sarajevo province -- the city of Sarajevo and the province of Sarajevo stand in a different posture or was it proposed that it be handled differently than some of the other proposed provinces?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And, briefly, how so?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The province of Sarajevo which comprised the city and the surrounding areas was to have a more structured tripartite consensual rule as between the Bosnian Croats, the Bosnian Muslims, and the Bosnian Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And is it fair to say that it was -- it was to be less identified and none of the -- as I understand what you have told me, what others have told me, none of the provinces were to be ethnic as such but that the Sarajevo province even less so?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. If I might expand on that briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The essence of the Vance-Owen Peace Plan in all of its parts, the map, the constitutional principles, the military arrangements and later the suggestions for an interim government, the essence of the plan was multi-ethnicity, decentralisation, consensual decision-making and democracy. And actually, you can see that if you look -- if one were to look at the population of the 10 provinces. To begin with, four of them had no ethnic majority whatsoever, and then the overall picture was as follows: 36 per cent of the entire Bosnian Serb population of Bosnia-Herzegovina was outside the Bosnian Serb majority provinces, 36 per cent. 30 per cent of the Bosnian Muslim population resided outside the Muslim majority provinces, and 29 per cent of the Bosnian Croat population of the country resided outside the Bosnian Croat majority provinces, and that was done consciously to emphasise the multi-ethnic aspect along with the other features that Lord Owen mentioned in his remarks, the geography, et cetera. So I think that makes it clear that the multi-ethnic aspect was -- was a dissideratum of the peace plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And with that if we could turn to the copy of the map as it is laid out in these materials or contained in these materials on page 19 of the exhibit. And, Your Honour, for the next -- for some time this afternoon we're going to be working with a number of maps and I -- it may get to be a bit -- well, I don't want to say confusing, but we may be going from one map to another and hope everyone will bear with us in doing that. It may be that anyone in the courtroom to look at a larger map, it is -- this same map is map 11 in the Prosecution's book of maps, which is Exhibit P 09276, map 11, the Vance-Owen Peace Plan, 2 January 1993, and page 12 of that exhibit in e-court. I simply give people the choice of using the larger coloured map or the smaller map that's in the materials itself on page 19.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: There is a third map, Your Honour, and this is the map that will we had given notice over the weekend that we would be using, and it is a map, and I'll ask the Ambassador to confirm. If the Ambassador could also be provided if he doesn't have one now, Exhibit P 09841. And if the usher doesn't have one, we have an extra one here.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, if you'll look at the map, this additional map that has just been placed in front of you, Exhibit P 09841. Can you just confirm for the record this is a map in fact that you had provided me over this past weekend; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is the final Vance-Owen map. The UN version is the January map. This was the map developed, and it was the map after March 25, when the Bosnian Muslim government approved it and signed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. For current purposes, I'm not going to look at the differences so much of the January happen map and the March map, but we will come to that in the course of the afternoon. But because of the additional information on this map, can you just confirm that what Exhibit P 09841 does is to impose the Vance-Owen proposed provincial borders onto a demographic map of Bosnia-Herzegovina based upon the 1991 census?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I would not use the word "impose." They were not imposed on the parties. They were developed by the parties in conversations with the negotiators.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I appreciate that. I probably -- when I said "imposed," I should say the borders overlaid on the map, just physically on the map itself as opposed to imposed on the parties. The borders have been laid over, if you will, the demographic map; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Likewise, Your Honour, I'll just mention for purposes of the record and again to assist anyone in the courtroom, in the Prosecution's book of maps, P 09276, map number 9, page 10 in e-court, is a map showing the ethnic composition of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Again, simply another version that the Prosecution submits is basically consistent with the map we're looking at now, but if anyone in the courtroom wants to use one or the other, they might be able to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, when you look at map -- the map that has now been marked -- which you provided me, as Exhibit P 09841, do you see that the proposed 8 and 10 include or encompass a substantial amount of Muslim majority areas or, to put it the other way around, includes a substantial amount of territory where the Croats were neither a majority or a plurality?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: When you -- then next refer you and the courtroom --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: The witness will need be provided with the book, the booklet of maps, please. The usher can provide just one more map that's only in this book at the moment. Map 7. Sorry, it's map number -- it's -- excuse me, map number 6. It's page 7 in e-court. Excuse me. Your Honour, in the book -- Your Honours, in the book of maps, map 6 is the map in the Prosecution's book of exhibits, maps that are -- has the -- both the Banovina overlay on the map of parts of Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina and also on -- showing the borders of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, Ambassador, I've now put a number of maps in front of you, and let me ask you this: When you compared the maps in the Vance-Owen Plan in January, the book -- the map that is on page 19 of the materials, and you compare that map to the map 6 that I've just put in front of you, can you tell us what relationship or correspondence you see between Vance-Owen provinces 8 and 10 and the claimed borders of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna and the part of the 1939 Banovina extending into Western Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's clear what one compares the map, the Banovina map, that's your map number 6 in your book, and the map in the UN document, which has the Vance-Owen Plan, the original map, that they are basically the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And with all this -- with all these maps and that information in front of us now, and perhaps a bit fresher than when we finished yesterday, based on all that, can you remind the Judges what was then the reaction to the Bosnian Croat party to the Vance-Owen proposals as presented in January 1993?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were enthusiastic, particularly about the map, but about the entire plan. They signed all three parts of the package, the map, the constitutional principles, and the military arrangements at once. They signed with alacrity.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you give us from your experience at the time and being closely involved in this process of your analysis or assessment of the reasons that they agreed so quickly to this map both as expressed to you and based upon what you knew about the process?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they were pleased with the map, which was generous to the Bosnian Croat community. We thought it was fair, but it was also generous. The constitutional principles they did not like any more than the Bosnian Serbs liked them, and the military arrangements they were already violating, but they signed in the secure knowledge that the Bosnian Serbs and to a lesser degree the Bosnian Muslims would not agree with the package, and therefore they were able to get a free ride. They were free riders, so to speak, to use the economic expression, on -- on the situation, and they were in -- in a secure position.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me turn to a different aspect of the proposals as they existed in January, that is the topic of separation of forces. Can I ask you, in looking back at the document for a moment -- we're looking away from the maps for the moment so it's not as urgent for people to have those in front of them at the moment but if you go back to Exhibit P 09852, the packet of Vance-Owen material for January 1993, can I please direct your attention to page 17, again numbered page 17 at the top, paragraph number 8. You mentioned this, I believe, yesterday, but to bring us into the next topic, is it correct that one of the 10 fundamental or constitutional principles was number 8: "Bosnia and Herzegovina is to be progressively demilitarised under United Nations/European Community supervision"?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was -- you're correct, and it was a very important provision.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can I ask you please now to go to page 20 of the document of Annex number IV. But it's on page 20.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: My page 20 says Annex number VI.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I think you're right. I think you're absolutely right. Let me just double-check. Yes, that's correct. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, during this break it might be good if my learned friend could repeat the number of the document because there is an error in the transcript and it would be good to have it on record. It will be important so as not to waste time later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Exhibit P 09852, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And you are absolutely correct. It is Annex VI on page 20. This is called agreement for peace in Bosnia and Herzegovina. And again on that page and I'm going to take you through a series of references until we get to some particular language that I have questions, but just so everyone in the courtroom can follow for process, if I can ask you to look at paragraph number 4 toward the bottom of that page. "Arrangements on the separation of forces as set out in Annex IV to the present agreement." So then we need to turn to Annex IV to this agreement. It should be on page -- well, actually, before we do that, sorry, sorry, because there's another related topic that I want to indicate. If you go to page 22 first, which is Annex I. Don't worry so much about the annex numbers for the moment but just the page number, page 22. And if I can direct your attention again to Annex I, cessation of hostilities, and we're not going to read the entire page, but as you scan down the page you'll see that in the third -- roughly the third paragraph overall on the page a cease-fire must be put in place and remain effective. This is to be implemented 72 hours from the time of signature of the agreement. It talks about monitoring by UN protection force, ECMM. It says the separation of forces is to be achieved, et cetera. On the next page, again reference to such things as establish the demarcation line, move in United Nations Protection Forces to establish security. Down below on the page again separations of forces. Second item, area of separation to be agreed. Do you see all that, and is that again, as you recall, the basic concepts that were being offered or proposed at the time?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This concerned the immediate end of hostilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes. Now, with that in mind, more specifically then if we can go to it, page 30, specifically separation of forces. Annex IV. Again under steps such things as an absolute cease-fire. Next, temporary freezing of the military situation, pending agreement on the return of forces to designated provinces. "No forward deployments or offensive action." Control measures some examples, monitoring of front lines, establishing lines on which forces may be located. Staged withdrawal of forces culminating with their location to designated provinces. And again is that part of the process, the proposal as you understood it at the time?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me, with that background in mind, then, take you back to Lord Owen's opening statement on page 11 overall. And his -- his statement starts on page 11 but then continues over to page 12 and 13. If I can ask you to look please at the bottom of page 12 the paragraph starting with the words "Separation of the armed forces." Might I just ask you, sir, rather than myself reading it, could you just read that paragraph out loud?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It reads and I quote: "Separation of the armed forces throughout Bosnia and Herzegovina will have to be negotiated in the light of the boundaries of the new provinces. It is envisaged that there will be no military forces in Sarajevo province. Bosnian Serb forces might withdraw to provinces 2, 4, and 6. Bosnian Croat forces could be deployed in province 3, and the remaining forces would hopefully reach agreement as to their deployment in provinces 1, 5, 8, 9, and 10. Under our constitutional principles, number 8, Bosnia and Herzegovina is to be progressively demilitarised."

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, sir, the various passage that I've just referred to you and to the courtroom and this statement by Lord Owen, can you confirm to the Chamber for purposes of other questions this afternoon, are those the entire provisions or a sampling of the entire provisions, because we saw that we didn't read every item on every page, of what the Vance-Owen proposals as of early January proposed in this regard?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct, as of -- as of the January proposal.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, if we look at the map, and whichever one of the Vance-Owen proposals at the time, whichever one people want to use but using the one at page 19 and referring back to Lord Owen's opening statement, he's saying that the Bosnian Serb forces might withdraw to provinces 2, 4, and 6. People can see where those roughly are. Bosnian Croat forces could be deployed in province 3. There's province 3 up in the upper right area of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Is that -- does that correspond roughly to the Posavina?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is the Posavina province.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And that the remaining forces would hopefully reach agreement as to their deployment in provinces 1, 5, 8, 9, and 10. Basically meaning all that was subject to further agreement among the parties.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And finally before leaving this document, just to put the time factor into further context, can I ask you to look at page 4 of the document. In the bottom half of that page, sir, in the section that's headed "Plenary Session on the 4th of January, 1993," refers then to a Plenary Session on the 4th of January, and then if I can direct your attention to paragraph 20, lower on the page. Is it correct that then, that at the end of the 4th of January the conference or the proceedings were recessed until the 10th of January?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And is that fact consistent with what actually happened?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'd have to consult my diary to see whether it's completely consistent, but I suspect it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. And in fact on that regard if we can go back then to some of your diary entries, and if I can ask you to look, please, at Exhibit P 01038, which is in binder 1. These are the diary excerpts or diary items that we were looking at yesterday. It should be in one of the --

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me, sir, what is that number?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I can ask you to turn to your entries on the -- for the 10th of January, 1993, which according to your -- to the document we were just looking at would have been the next day that meetings were held after a period of recess. And if I can direct your attention in particular, again using the numbers that we were using yesterday, and I appreciate again they are sometimes not the easiest thing to fine, but if you can find 4287, please, once you have found the 10th of January. 4287 which --

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I have located it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And for those using e-court, it's at page 35 of e-court. Excuse me, page 42. My apology. Page 42. Sorry, let me catch up with you, Ambassador. Thank you. Sorry. Sir, can you tell us then what commenced again or what were you doing according to these minutes or notes on the 10th of January, 1993?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The meeting on the 10th of January was a rolling series of negotiations with the parties. The page that you've referred to was with Mate Boban and both -- and Akmadzic. The meeting lasted from 7.25 p.m. until 8.00 p.m. in the evening, and we discussed with them their view of where things stood.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. And I don't -- because we need to move forward in time, and I think we may have touched -- we may have gotten about this far yesterday before stopping, but on this page does Boban -- do you have a note for Boban saying, "I believe the Muslims don't want a map at all. We must insist on constitutional text that Muslims accept map"?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And what was your understanding of the meaning of "much insist in constitutional text"?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mate Boban knew very well that the Bosnian Muslims wanted a centralised state with very small administrative units. If that's the case, the opstina map would suffice. You could just have counties and you wouldn't need any map at all. You don't, for example, have a map of New York State in the United States. That was the Muslim objective. There was no -- never any doubt of that. So that's what Mate Boban meant when he said the Muslims don't want a map at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Then if you turn -- I believe it should be, hopefully, the next page, 4297, using again the numbers, and for a meeting on the 12th of January, 1993. On the top left -- on the left side of the page, of course, in your journal, again, as we saw yesterday, we're basically looking at two pages, your journal opened using two pages. At the left side at the top, does this indicate a meeting on the 12th of January? You've written the notations, Mate Boban, Mile Akmadzic, General Petkovic.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Going to the right side of the page, about halfway down, do you see a section -- about the middle of the page some comments attributed to Mate Boban?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm afraid I don't. We're not on the same page.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, I'm sorry for that. Page 4297.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Did you mean 4297 or 87.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: This particular document is 4297.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: The -- 97. All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you. I have 4297. Yes, a comment by Boban.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Could you read that, please?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: "You will have great difficulties with Muslims on both the principles and the map. Give significance to what I say. Do not be caught off guard by the Muslims."

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And -- I'm sorry, I'm not sure we're still on the same page. Page 4297, your meeting on the 12th of January. Yes, I see where you were. Thank you very much. You're on the left side. Could I ask you to go across to the right side of the page?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: About the middle.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And other comments attributed to Mr. Boban, and can you read that, please.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: "We're running out of goodwill. We want to consult with you. We want a solution. We'll be waiting. Our people are worried, are losing patience with the Muslims. Tell Izzie," that is President Izetbegovic, "Tell Izzie that either Akmadzic remains as president of the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina, or the government will cease to exist." That's a quote, "Will cease to exist."

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sorry, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The Muslims in Sarajevo are trying to replace him," and then I put in parentheses my own comment, "Ganic?" Telling myself that perhaps they were trying to put Ejub Ganic in the place of Akmadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And just to pick up from yesterday when it makes reference here to being Akmadzic being president of the government, he was the Prime Minister at that time? He was in that position at the time?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was Prime Minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Now, up above that you said a moment ago -- let me just give -- let me just ask you to look at that again. You said, "We'll be waiting." Does it say "We'll be writing you? We'll be writing --"

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, excuse me. Yes, we'll be writing you. I beg your pardon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And above that says, "We're running out of goodwill"?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: What was your sense, Ambassador, and the sense of Lord Owen and Secretary Vance at this time as to the continued postures or patience of the various parties as you approached the middle of January 1993?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Bosnian Serbs, Karadzic, Koljevic, Krajisnik, and all of them were the most demanding, the least cooperative, and of course, in terms of military activities, they were doing the most damage, particularly to Sarajevo. The Bosnian Muslims were hanging on by their fingernails and hoping for the best. The Bosnian Croats were in the best position of the three parties, because they were organised already in Croatia, and they had a strong military force in Bosnia-Herzegovina, both strong and well-led, and they were anxious to get on with their business.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And what -- when Boban says, "Are losing patience with Muslims," what did you take from that?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they were nominal allies. After all, they were together in fighting the Serbs. But as we knew, and as Mate told us right here, "We're losing patience with the Muslims." We know they were anxious to clear the Muslims out of their -- you know, of what they considered their national homeland, Herceg-Bosna, and this occurred in January. Everybody was aware of what happened in Prozor two months earlier. So that -- we interpreted that that meant that if the Muslims didn't shape up and sign on board that there would be more displacement of Muslim people.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Before we leave this diary entry, again for the 12th of January, can I ask you to go back to the left side of the page, and above the portion you read a few minutes ago, the other statement attributed to Boban where he says, "You'll have great difficulties," but above that, could you read your entry immediately above that section starting with the word "earlier"?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a summary. It doesn't have the exact words of Akmadzic because you will note it is in parentheses.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I summarise the situation, and I write, and I quote: "Earlier, just before -- just before Boban arrived, Akmadzic told us Muslims had no legitimate complaints, and the map was generous to them. For example, Vares, a Croat town forever, was given to the Muslims."

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And what did you think about that statement? Was there anything about that statement that you thought was, well, noteworthy enough to put in your diary? With an asterisk.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in some respects it was accurate. Vares was a holy town to the Serbs [sic]. It was the site of the oldest Roman Catholic bishopric in the area. President Tudjman showed us that clearly and so it was a very sensitive city, and it was put into a Muslim majority province. So I think that's what he was pointing out, and that was the essence of his position.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. It may be worth if people -- if, Ambassador, you still have the packet of Vance-Owen materials next to you, Exhibit P 09852.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: The packet of documents, Your Honours, we were looking at a few minutes ago. It may be worth looking back at the map on page 19 of those materials?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: It might be worth correcting the record. He indicated this was a holy town to the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Excuse me, I didn't hear you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You indicated that Vares was a holy town to the Serbs. The Serbs are Orthodox.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Did I say that?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes, I believe that you misspoke, and I just --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, I beg your pardon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: On line 14.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Line 14 to the --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, of course it's Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I appreciate counsel catching that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Page -- I'm sorry. I can't believe I said it, but if the -- it the monitor shows it, I believe the monitor.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can I ask you then in looking back at -- at the map on page 19, does that indeed show that as of January 1993, and again the copy is not ideal, that's why the map and the book -- book of maps may be better for some things, but nonetheless, do you see that as of January 1993 Vares, the municipality of Vares, which is just immediately above or, if you will, say, north of the Sarajevo municipality, that was included in proposed province number 9?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have it in front of me, but I'm sure you're correct. It was --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I think it's also in the map -- out of the materials, the Vance-Owen materials on your right, I think you can also see --

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: But it doesn't show Vares. What is the Vance-Owen map in this document of yours?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'll be right with you.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Number 11, it's map number 11, and, for e-court, page 12 of Exhibit 09276.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Map number 11. Yes. I'm sorry to take the time of the Court. The Vares is indeed in province number 9, which was a Muslim majority province.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I can then next ask you to turn to Exhibit P 01158 in your set of materials. I believe it will be in binder number 1, which hopefully someone -- I think the same one you're in.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, this is a record, you will see, of a meeting with President Tudjman in Zagreb, and if you look on the first page it will indicate that apparently at about 1550 hours or 10 minutes to 4.00 that day on the 15th of January, 1993, President Franjo Tudjman welcome the co-chairmen Mr. Vance and Lord Owen, Ambassador Ahtisaari, President Izetbegovic, Boban, and his delegation to a meeting at the presidential offices; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you asking me?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I wasn't there so I'm just reading the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: This particular meeting, you did not accompany Mr. Vance and Lord Owen?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No I was in Geneva chairing -- chairing the conference.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me ask you just simply then to -- I'm going to ask you to look at page 48, ask you to go to page 48 of the transcript, please.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: On page 48, and I'm going to have to read a couple of pages to you in order to put the next sets of questions to you about this. Izetbegovic is speaking at this point on page 48. Izetbegovic says: "I will just take the floor once more and I won't take it again. I would say I agree with President Tudjman that this discussion should be finished. But I think it is necessary to resolve a misunderstanding here because I think it may be at the core of the fighting that has now happened in Gornji Vakuf, a misunderstanding, perhaps a misinterpretation of these documents. "So, for my part, with this I will finish this conversation, for my part. I don't think this conversation should go on, except for this item, which I think should be clarified. "It's about the interpretation of a paragraph from the documents put forward by Messrs. Vance and Owen. "So it's about the interpretation, about comprehending or understanding one of the items put forward in these documents. "Mr. Boban said he understood from these papers that the armies, that is -- excuse me, that each army should withdraw to their territories. That's not how I understood the papers and I don't know whether this was the intention of these documents, because I do not see that they define who has what territories, whose armies these are, you know. So I am afraid what is now going on in Gornji Vakuf may have been caused by a misunderstanding of this item of these agreements." Going on to the next page: "I am not sure I understood Mr. Boban correctly, but he seems to have understood say now that the Bosnia army should withdraw from the region, from the Travnik province now, and the HVO should take it over completely. I do not understand these papers like this." Tudjman says: "How else will have you the Serbs withdraw and leave? Izetbegovic: "Of course I'm only saying that this is not what these papers say now or when this moment starts. Of course there will be such moves but it has to be defined. I do not think this has been defined in the papers yet nor has the movement for it been set. I'm afraid that such a reading of these papers or this provision and Mr. Boban that such a reading may have caused the clashes in Gornji Vakuf. Perhaps he wants the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina to withdraw from there now, but since it is not doing so then it should be driven out. "Boban: "No, that's not how things are set up." Izetbegovic: "I think because you, Mate, said it a few moments ago, hasn't withdrawn [as read] been foreseen?" Boban: "I said you should tell your people that provinces 10 and 13," 13 may be an error but that's what the transcript says, but "10 and 13 have been agreed on between the Croats and the Muslims and there won't be any problems for you to do it, like I did on TV when I appealed for peace, brotherhood, cooperation, co-existence between the Muslims and the Croats and for bridging the gap at all costs. You do it and there will be peace." Izetbegovic: "I don't think this was foreseen in any of these proposals. It was not foreseen that the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina should leave either the Travnik province or Mostar. That's not how I understood these papers. I am not sure that's what is written there." "It seems to me, I'm sorry, Mate, that this is how you understood it and that's not how you understood it ..." Boban: That's how I understood it." It goes on. Tudjman talks again. Susak talks a bit. And if I can direct in the interests of time to page 52, toward of end of this conversation, of course anyone can read any more -- the entire record is in the transcript. Anyone can refer to any additional parts of it they wish. David Owen on page 52. You find that. And Owen says at the end, toward the end of the meeting: "I think this has been a very useful discussion although we have not reached any definite conclusions. I think the one and only real way to reach any solution is by discussing these issues. "With regard to individual provinces, I said while explaining the system that the Serbian military forces would withdraw to the provinces of Banja Luka, Bijeljina, and Eastern Herzegovina. "I did not make any suggestions about the others, but I think I mentioned that this was an issue for the BH army and the HVO to discuss together." Now, before I put a broader question to you, what Lord Owen says there at the end, does he provide an accurate summary of what the Vance-Owen proposals were as of the middle of January 1993?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They were the proposals in the UN document that you read just a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And so when you read -- the part that I have read to you, sir, that I've pointed out to you starting at page 48, can you comment on whether you agree or disagree with the position and assessment stated by President Izetbegovic?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In this connection Izetbegovic is correct and Mate Boban has it wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Had there been any part of the Vance-Owen proposal as it existed as of mid-January that would require any ABiH forces to relocate from provinces 8 or 10?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can I ask you please to go to Exhibit P 01155. And, sir, this is a document titled "Decision," dated the 15th of January, 1993, signed by -- or over the name of, at least, Jadranko Prlic. Stamped. And I'll just ask you, please, to look at the document itself and, in particular, in the first paragraph it says: "In line with the agreements which were reached and signed at the International Conference on the former Yugoslavia ... The HVO of the HZ HB, the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, reached a decision at a special meeting in Mostar on the 15th of January 1993," that is that day. "Decision." And point number 1: "All units of the BH army currently in regions 3, 8, and 10 which were proclaimed Croatian in the Geneva agreements are subordinate to the command of the main headquarters of the HVO armed forces." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Going down to paragraph number 5: "The decision shall be implemented within five days starting from today, 15th of January, 1993," making that presumably the 20th of January. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: 6: "This decision shall be implemented by the head of the defence department of the HVO of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna." My question to you, is sir, a couple of questions. The document itself starts out with the words, "In line with the agreements reached and signed at the international conference ..." Were there any agreements that had been signed by all the parties, and was there any agreement in fact as of the 15th [Realtime transcript read in error "23rd"] of January, 1993?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The agreement as of January 15th you have already read to the Court. We have all looked at it. There is nothing in it that would permit this statement that the decision is in line. It's contrary to the agreement, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Before passing on to some other documents, if I can ask you to look at number 3, it says: "Units of the Kiseljak and Kresevo HVOs whose municipalities are in region 7, remain under the command of the main headquarters of the HVO ... until a final agreement has been reached on the status of region 7." Now, can you provide any insight or information to the Chamber on -- in all of what is stated here in this decision by Mr. Prlic on the 15th of January, why was an exception being made for the HVO units in the Kiseljak region?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Kiseljak and Kresevo, as we can see from your map of the Vance-Owen Plan and province 7 are in the province we call Sarajevo province, and as we've discussed earlier, separate arrangements, political, military, administrative, were made for the Sarajevo province, essentially providing for consensus of all three parties on all aspects of the organisation of the province, that is to say political, economic, and military.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I've been -- I've been -- it's been pointed out to me that on line 12 of page 27 there's an error. It should say there were in fact any agreements by the 15th of January, and for some reason the transcript says the 23rd of January. If we could correct that, please. And the witness has it correct when he goes on to say the agreement as of January 15th.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Going further from that interruption, sir, but let me ask you this in connection again with paragraph number 3 and Kiseljak and what you have you just said about Sarajevo. Were there terms or conditions or agreements to the Sarajevo province any more firm or final or agreed to as they were as to provinces 8 and 10?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the -- excuse me. The Sarajevo province was understandably in many respects the most sensitive province. It was the capital of the country. It was being besieged by the Serbs. We know that. And it was to be the capital of the future unified sovereign state so that separate arrangements were envisaged for the Sarajevo province.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Although they had not been finalised as of the 15th of January; is that correct? But still there was no agreement. There was still no Vance-Owen agreement?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. The Serbs had not signed onto anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, I was going to refer to the similar or related orders on the 15th of January signed by Mr. Stojic, Exhibit P 01140, and then in turn by Mr. Petkovic, P 01156, but I believe the Chamber has seen those before and, in the interest of time, I'm not going to go into them now unless the Chamber wishes to.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Could I ask you to next look at, then, Exhibit P 01150. Sir, this is a document that purports to be -- that sets out an order that was given, allegedly given, by a man named Bozo Rajic on the 16th of January, 1993. Do you recall who Mr. Rajic -- what his position he held at that time?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was defence minister, as I recollect.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And defence minister of what entity?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And do you recall whether Mr. Rajic was a Muslim or a Croat or Serb?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a -- I believe he was a Croat.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And do you see that in his order, paragraph 1, are specific in particular as to provinces 3, 8, and 10, that he was indicating that again the -- essentially the ABiH should be subordinated to the HVO in those provinces?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And let me ask you then to next turn to 11 -- Exhibit P 01168. I'll just show you a couple of documents before I ask some questions about them. Exhibit P 01168 appears to be an order dated the same day, the 16th of January, 1993, in which the commander of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the ABiH, Mr. Halilovic, and the -- the main paragraph being paragraph number 1 under his order essentially directs the ABiH not to in fact subordinate themselves to the control of the HVO HZ HB; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Above that, when Mr. Halilovic gives the reasoning for his order the -- in the text above the line where it says "Command," it says: "Regarding the facts that the talks in Geneva had not been finished yet and all sides in talks have not signed the documents offered, we consider the above-mentioned decisions directly endanger further mutual fight against the aggressor." Was General Halilovic's analysis accurate that, in fact, there were no -- there was no agreement as of that time?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he's accurate. May I add something?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: But even if the agreements were complete, that is to say if the Vance-Owen Plan of -- as of January 15 had been signed by all three parties in all of its parts, the actions taken by the HVO would have been illegal and contrary to the agreement because there was nothing in the agreement that -- that said what -- what the HVO was claiming.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Very well. Can I next ask you to look at Exhibit P 01267. And do you see that this is a letter Mr. Izetbegovic to Jadranko Prlic, president of the HVO, and does it stated -- is it stated again in the first paragraph, excuse me, second sentence: "Until final agreement about the future constitution about Bosnia-Herzegovina is reached in Geneva, our opinion is that all unilateral acts should be avoided by all parties, including your decision on subordination of the B and H army/HVO units in certain provinces". And again, can I simply ask you what President Izetbegovic says here, is that consistent with what the Vance-Owen -- is his position supported by the Vance-Owen proposals as they existed at the time?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. What President Izetbegovic says is in conformity with the Vance-Owen Plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me ask you to look next at Exhibit P 01263. And this appears to be a response by Mr. Prlic to the letter of Mr. Izetbegovic that we were just looking at. I might just give you a moment, please, for you to look at the letter, and perhaps others in the courtroom, to see what the letter is. Perhaps you can just look up at any point that you're -- you're sufficiently familiar with it. Yes.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Well, the president of the HVO of Herceg-Bosna, Dr. Prlic, takes issue, strong issue, with the position stated earlier by Izetbegovic and General Halilovic, namely that their Vance-Owen Plan does not call for the unilateral subordination of the BH army to the HVO in the three named provinces, and he restates the Bosnian Croat position, and he's incorrect, that it's just not the fact. It's an assertion, but he is incorrect.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And just to look at one specific sentence, in fact the last sentence of Dr. Prlic's letter, "you already know this is in accordance with the Geneva documents." And as you just answered this, was these positions set out by Dr. Prlic at this time in fact in accordance with the Geneva documents?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The opposite was the case. It was totally not in accordance with the Geneva documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can I ask you next to look at Exhibit P 01192. And I'll ask you to look at that for a moment. It says it's a decision dated the 18th of January, 1993, by Jadran Topic, who was the president of the Mostar municipal HVO.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In the body of his -- the first "I" section of his decision again it says: "In accordance with the Geneva accords and the introduction of civilian power, all appointments in economic and public organisations and institutions in Mostar municipality made by the commanders of the BH army units and all legal effects (contracts, decisions ...)" and so on, "of these appointments shall be rendered invalid on the day this decision comes into effect," which it says on item 3 is the 18th of January, 1993. Now once again, sir, to your knowledge as a close and active participant in the Vance-Owen process, was there anything in the Vance-Owen process and as it existed in mid-January which was consistent with the action taken by Mr. Topic?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, nothing. We have the Vance-Owen Plan in front of us, and if one wanted to read the entire plan you could see that there is nothing in the plan that would lead to this kind of a statement. This statement and the previous ones violate both the letter and the spirit of the Vance-Owen Plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can I ask you, please, next to go to Exhibit P 01343. And just to finish up this particular series of documents. Is this a decision by President Izetbegovic to essentially invalidate the order that had been issued by Bozo Rajic that we look at a few minutes ago about the subordination of the ABiH units to the HVO?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is it. And he -- President Izetbegovic also had a note, I don't have did in front of me, but about the same time declaring null and void the -- another document that was issued by the defence minister. Or am I -- am I referring -- thinking of the same document perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm not sure, sir, Ambassador, at the moment?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think we've seen so many documents that all make the same point, but they came from various chains --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- in the Bosnian Croat command. So excuse me for --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You're right?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- confusing --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You're right and as we had said earlier we didn't look at them all. In the chain of command there were orders -- similar orders issued by Mr. Stojic and Mr. Petkovic, but I think the Chamber had seen those before and so simply I didn't dwell on them at this juncture. If I could ask you then to move forward to the 20th of January, the document we just looked at, the decision by Mr. -- President Izetbegovic being on the 19th of January. Could I ask you to look in your diary, Exhibit P 01038? And your entries for the --

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me, what is that number?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes. 1038. It should be in the first binder, and we're looking -- the date of the entry will be the 20th of January. And in particular -- I think the first entry that you'll actually be looking at will be 43 --

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: That's all right. If you can find 4315. If you have 43 --

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have 4315.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And looking at this page, can you just remind us and put in context then what -- basically what was continuing? What were you doing, you and Secretary Vance and Lord Owen doing around the 20th of January, 1993?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, January 20 was a very important, very busy, and very frustrating day because of the documents that you've introduced in the Court, this unilateral Bosnian Croat decision to subordinate the Bosnian army to the HVO in the provinces that they called their provinces, and all this back and forth, and you've read it, the letters between Izetbegovic and Prlic's letter, all of that. The co-chairmen decided to bring all the parties together to see if they could resolve this, because while this was going on, there was pretty heavy fighting. The HVO was -- was clearing out Muslim civilians from these areas, and the situation was worsening so that the co-chairmen, Secretary Vance and Lord Owen, urgently brought everybody together on January 20 in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can I ask you to then look specifically -- excuse me one moment. Well, it's still on the 20th, but I'm afraid for -- if I can ask you to go back several -- couple of pages to 4312. My apology for that, but it's -- if you just flip back a couple of pages to the page number 4312.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Again on the left-hand side of your journal as laid open here about -- on the bottom of the half. Page there are some notations for -- attributed to AK. Who is that?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Akmadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And what do you write in your diary on that lower part of the page?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I should introduce by saying that this -- this meeting was extremely contentious, and at times degenerated into a shouting match, the arguments between the Bosnian Croats and the Bosnian Muslims. It was quite an experience. We all remembered it, because coincidentally it was the day that President Clinton was being sworn in. January 20th is an important date for the Americans, and so it stuck in our minds because this -- this extremely hostile meeting. Akmadzic had with him written notes. He had a prepared statement that he took out of his pocket, and he said, "We, our Croat people, were attacked bit Muslim troops. The HVO defence was a legal one. We asked for an order from the defence minister, i.e., that armed forces should withdraw to provinces per Geneva. We want to start implementing what we have signed. We have no interest in continuing this war. We want a cease-fire and a just peace. If not possible in all of Bosnia-Herzegovina, then where we are a majority. If we agree here, we are ready to issue an order for a cease-fire and cessation of hostilities. We are ready for a cease-fire and to make a public statement, but we -- but not ready to agree what was agreed in Geneva. All we want is that the Muslim side accept the documents from Geneva completely." That's a quote. "All we want is that the must side accept the documents from Geneva completely, or at least in part but we would like them to agree on provincial structures so we can implement the Geneva peace plan."

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Then your next entry there is Boras?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Boras was a senior Croat leader.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And what is said there?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says: "The HVO has offered the other side," that is the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and that's in quotes the other side, the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, that at Gornji Vakuf both sides should withdraw and the security of people would be in the hands of a mixed police force."

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Then could you please then -- Izetbegovic is IZ, Izetbegovic, and does he make a response?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He says: "Won't go into reasons for the conflict, but the defence minister's order a unilateral act was the cause," meaning was the cause of the fighting. "Was opposed by the army of BiH to be withdrawn." The act -- meaning the act -- the statement by the Defence minister was to be withdrawn. The words are "act to be withdrawn."

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Let me direct your attention -- we're coming up on the time for the break. Let me direct your attention across the page, and toward the end of that particular part of the conversation, does Lord Owen make an intervention?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before or after?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: After. Across the page, on the right side of your journal, do you see an entry for DLO?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, yes. I see it now. Speaking personal -- well, Owen, was agreeing with Izetbegovic and he says, "Speaking personally, I think the defend minister's statement was premature. That proves the defects in your government structure. If the defence minister, not the Presidency but the army's CIC is no -- there was no HVO member in the Presidency. Let the defence minister's instruction lie and not be implemented until further discussions have taken place."

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And what was Akmadzic's response?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Akmadzic responds: "It will so lie."

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And Haris Silajdzic is the man you identified yesterday, and what does he add then to the conversation?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Silajdzic was the number two on the Bosnian Muslim side, and he said: "The cause of the problem is those who understand the provinces as national space. The Muslims were massacred in Prozor two months ago. We have the names of those criminals who did it. The same thing will -- some same thing is happening or will happen in Gornji Vakuf," et cetera, et cetera. And Owen says: "Okay. No withdrawal," meaning no subordination of the Bosnian government army to the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: UN to monitor.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: UN to monitor.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And just to finish on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And then, Your Honour, I suggest that we could take a break.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: But on that day and if I can direct you back to -- one moment, please. Actually, if you'd turn down a couple of pages until you get to page 4315. Again still on the 20th.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: On the bottom right side of that page did you note any comments, your personal comments, about that particular meeting?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The meeting ended at 4.05 p.m. You can see I draw a line under it with a cross which is my fashion, and then I write "comment," which is my comment on what has gone before, and it reads: "Extremely revealing meeting. Hostility level very high. Also invective. Muslim-Croat alliance, cooperation, collaboration, next to non-existent. Government and Presidency -- fig leaf, tiny and transparent." And then I characterise the individual behaviour. If you would like me to read it, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sure, we'll finish with that.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Izetbegovic was composed, worried, in charge. Haris Silajdzic unhelpful, delusional, lying. Pejanovic role playing, pretending to be the honest broker. Akmadzic rigid, nervous, reading Boban's script. Boras smooth and pseudo-conciliatory. Lasic tough, hates the Muslims." And I made a note, a marginal note on the side where, if I may, I can read that. It's three words.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wrote in Russian because it was January 20th, I mentioned President Clinton was being inaugurated, I wrote: "Clinton, be careful. Clinton [B/C/S spoken]. Clinton, be careful." Because it was a well-known fact that Clinton was going to be more interventionist in the Yugoslav portfolio than the previous administration, and so I was preparing to warn the administration that they were -- that they needed to be careful.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Ambassador?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think that's time for the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's time to have our break now. We'll resume in 20 minutes' time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, if I can direct you to -- I don't think we're going to have too many additional diary entries, but if I can ask you to go to Exhibit P 01275, 1275, another instalment, I think, of your diaries.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If you find your entry for the -- your entries for the 23rd of January, 1993. In particular I believe it's page 4331.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Already. If you have that, on the left side of the, again, page of your journal you have summit meeting of the five delegations. Are we on the same page?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Across from that -- well, did you just briefly set the scene for us as to what was happening, what this meeting was?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this was a very important, a major meeting. We've -- the last session before the break here in the court you have gone through the situation from the 15th to the 20th, the heavy fighting, the letters between the Muslims and the Bosnian Croats, the unilateral order issued by the defence minister, the -- President Izetbegovic's declaring it illegal and that sort of thing, ending with the shouting match between Akmadzic and Izetbegovic on January 20, that meeting that I -- that we just finished with. So given the inconclusive, not to say negative result of the January 20 meeting between the three parties, we decided to bring in formally the delegations, then the chiefs, from Croatia, from the Republic of Croatia, and from the then Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, which comprised Serbia and Montenegro, and they were all present and you can see the delegations were headed the Bosnian Muslims, Izetbegovic; the Serb Karadzic; Mate Boban in the chair for the Bosnian Croats, because President Tudjman, since he had a delegation from Croatia, was there with Susak, Radic, General Tus, who was the commander in chief of the armed forces of the Republic of Croatia, an airman, General Tus, formally -- before Croatia declared independence he had been the commander of the air force of the Yugoslav republic before he went to Croatia. And then for the federal republic, you see Cosic, Milosevic. Dobrica Cosic was the president of Yugoslavia at the time. Milosevic was the President of Serbia at that time, so down the list.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Let me ask you again partly because of the limitations of time, to go across the -- directly across the page, the right side, and you make -- there are three items there, 1, 2, 3 attributed I believe to Izetbegovic. Can you just read those Izetbegovic re: map. Read those three items.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Izetbegovic says read the map we have five objections one we cannot agree that the regions where ethnic cleansing took place could even be temporarily under the control of the cleansers. It does not matter that demilitarisation helps. "2. Also, while the conference goes on, and I quote, he said the aggression continues and is even intensifying." Sarajevo, Mostar, Yugoslav artillery bombardment. "3. Impossible to talk peace while the aggression continues."

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Is it fair to say that even by the 23rd of January then there was -- there was no agreement -- among other things there was still no agreement on the map?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And finally on this particular meeting if I can ask you to turn a few pages down, about three or four pages further into the journal until you find page 4334. Still on the 23rd of January. You begin a series of minutes --

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: -- then at three -- 330, I believe. Further down that page you have an item referenced it appears to be Izetbegovic. "Izetbegovic questions whole exercise and says if it's ethnicity he'll quit." What was that about?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this was a subsidiary meeting to the large meeting, and Martti Ahtissari was in the chair, as I've indicated, and he raised the matter of province number and the border with 3 -- with 9 and 10. Karadzic asks for more, meaning more land. Boban says he's satisfied with the border as drawn, and that was no surprise since indeed we knew that the Bosnian Croats were pleased with the map. Izetbegovic questions the whole exercise and says if it's ethnicity he'll quit. It meant he'll leave the talks if the ethnic principle becomes emphasised in the provincial structure because, as I mentioned earlier it was not in the provincial structure. It never was, actually. I gave you the figures of the population of the three parties, roughly a third for all of them but they were outside their provinces, et cetera, et cetera. So this was always very much on the Muslim mind, because both the Bosnian Serbs and the Bosnian Croats were emphasising the ethnic aspect.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Very well. I think we have to go forward to another exhibit, please. If I could ask you to turn to Exhibit P 01338. Just finishing up on January, a couple of items. 1338. And indeed, Ambassador, this may have been the additional document that -- that you were thinking of before the break. I don't know if it is, but it might be. This is a letter written from General Halilovic, dated the 28th of January, 1993, to the head of the defence department of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. Can I just ask you to look at the second paragraph of his letter. Read that to yourself. I'll just ask you a question or two about that.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Ambassador, similar to some of the questions I've asked you earlier this afternoon about other exchanges of views or correspondence between various parties, can you tell us in this particular instance do you agree with or is General Halilovic's assessment or analysis correct at least in this particular situation?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he's correct in what he states.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And could I ask you next to go to Exhibit P 01329. One moment, please. Actually, if you'll go to 1 -- excuse me a moment. Sorry. It's 1329. And can you just confirm, by the end of January 1993 whether in fact a cease-fire was obtained in connection with the fighting that had then broken out in January, and do you recall generally a cease-fire being agreed by President Izetbegovic and Mate Boban around this time?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was agreed but it was never put into effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Also, can I ask you next to turn to Exhibit 1363. That is P 01363. And can you tell us during this time, sir, were you and Secretary Vance and Lord Owen and others continuing to try to negotiate and bring the parties to agreement?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The negotiations indeed were more intense in January and particularly in this period because of the fighting around Gornji Vakuf and in Central Bosnia in general.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. And if we look at Exhibit 1363, can you just tell us what that is and what that indicates in terms of any further progress that you had been able to accomplish by that time?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the principal achievement that's set forth in that document which, as you can see, is essentially the constitutional framework which we've seen quite a lot of earlier --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- the three sides agreed. It was signed by Izetbegovic, Karadzic, and Mate Boban. So we had full agreement for the first time on the constitutional principles.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Earlier -- in an earlier version we saw that there had been 10 principles, and I note now there are only nine. Can you explain how that came about?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, one -- two were combined into one.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me next ask you to go to P 01285. And, sir, I'd just like you to read the first two paragraphs, number 1 and number 2 of this document, which is an UNPROFOR -- it says "Subject special assessment, Croat intentions for provinces 3, 8 and 10," dated the 24th of January, 1993. And if you could again please read paragraphs 1 and 2.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you want me to lead them aloud or to myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Read them aloud.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Paragraph 1: "Since the Geneva talks in early January, tensions are steadily increased between elements of both the Croat HVO and the principally Muslim army of Bosnia-Herzegovina (BH) in Central and Southern BH. Discord between their elements seems to occur," I can't quite see that last word, "seems to surface," excuse me. "Discord between them seems to surface every time the pressure from Bosnian Serb forces lulls and is significantly related to ethnic perceptions of the peace plan." Paragraph 2: "The tensions seem to be more severe in areas where there is no clear majority of either ethnic group in a particular opstina. This does not prevent areas like Prozor (majority Croat) or Jablanica (majority Muslim) from experiencing the effects of ethnic turmoil. Over the past week, the political and military leaders of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna have begun to implement their 'understanding' of the proposed settlement for the conflict in BH. This premature and imperfect grab for control of provinces 3, 8, and 10 has resulted in extremely high tensions in these and adjoining areas, and heavy fighting between Muslim and Croat units in and around Gornji Vakuf."

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And, sir, my question to you again is: As one of the architects of the Vance-Owen Plan and what you saw happening at the time, would you agree or disagree with the assessment stated in this UNPROFOR report?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's precisely correct in every point.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you tell us, sir, is it correct that the negotiations continued on into February and toward the latter part of March 1993?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they continued until May 1993, so, yes, they certainly continued in February and March, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. And we are going to come momentarily to the -- in fact, we are there now, to the 25th of March, 1993, and was there substantial further progress made or accomplished as of the 25th or 26th of March, 1993?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. March 25 was an important date because following the revisions to the plan during January, February, and March, on March 25 Izetbegovic signed all three sections of the plan on behalf of the Bosnian government. That is to say he agreed with the map, which had been altered since January. He agreed to the military arrangements, and he agreed to the constitutional principles.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So, finally, is it correct to say that you then had the signatures or agreement of two of the three parties to the various parts of the Vance-Owen package?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
