utterances.text: That is correct. I should also add, however, that Izetbegovic's agreement and signature was heavily qualified and conditioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you give the Chamber some sense of that? Qualified or conditioned in what ways?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, they were the usual Izetbegovic style, complaining about this or that and if the aggressor does this, we'll do that. It was no surprise.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I think we will have -- I think some of his correspondence or conditions or statements in the documents that --

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: They are in the documents. You can read the conditions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. You said a moment ago that there had been -- by the end of March there had been changes in the map. Can you briefly -- I don't know how many, but perhaps the most significant changes you recall in the map at that time?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was one significant change, and that was, if I may draw, your attention --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Actually -- sorry, Ambassador, if I can interrupt you for a second. My apology. If I can ask you to look a be if you still have available to you Exhibit P 09841 which was your map of the regions on the -- I think I see it probably on the bottom of everything this. The one we were looking at earlier today.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: You've given me a lot of paper, Counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I have. I have a habit of doing that.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: So I notice.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If you have in front of you, and I see that you do, P 09841, can you indicate for the Judges on that map any significant changes that had been made to the map by the end of March?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the one significant change is in the upper right-hand corner of the map between provinces 3 and 4 and 5. You will recall that the original Vance-Owen map of January did not have that finger that goes in -- of green that -- can I point it out somehow?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Not unless we put to be the ELMO?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, we can put it on the ELMO. Either way.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: What the new map did was give the Muslims access to the Sava River, thereby breaking the Serb corridor.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You may be able to indicate for us now, if the technology works correctly.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ah, yes. There it is. That's the new area. The Serb corridor was the most sensitive military area as far as General Mladic and the Serbs were concerned because it connected Belgrade to Banja Luka, and the original map had already broken the corridor by province 3, a Croat majority province. But the Bosnian Muslims were concerned about Croat-Serb collusion, so they wanted their own break in the corridor, and that's the area I coloured in, which gave them access to the Sava River.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. And before we move off of this exhibit and then we'll ask that the document as marked be given an IC number, but before we do that can I ask you about one other change to the map and looking at the map? If you look at province number 7, and that's the Sarajevo province; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Is it correct, sir, that by the end of March 1993, Vares, Visoko, Breza, and part of Kakanj had been moved out of the Muslim province number 9 and placed instead in Sarajevo province 7?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They were taken because of Bosnian Croat concerns, as I've indicated earlier when I misspoke and said Serb, you'll recall I mentioned that the Bosnian Croats had a deep and abiding affection for Vares because of the bishopric. So it was moved by us from a Muslim majority province to the Sarajevo province, which, as I mentioned earlier, required consensus on all decisions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, could we have a -- when a print of this marked version of this can be made it's based on P 09841 but if a new exhibit an IC number can be given to that, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Would you like me to mark it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be received in e-court as IC 521.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sort of -- that's roughly the ...

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I see for the record you've marked over red that encompasses the area we talked about, Vares, and some parts of Kakanj that you've marked on the map?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes it's an approximate marking, you understand. I'm not a cartographer.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Very well. If we've done, if we've accomplished all that, please can I then ask you to go to Exhibit P 01398 [Realtime transcript read in error "03198"].

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hmm. Yes, I have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'll just represent for the record, sir, and perhaps you can just confirm, this is a packet of Security Council official records covering certain materials for January, February, March 1993, and if I can ask you to turn in that document until you get to what would be using the pages that are actually on the document. Although they're not all continuous, but if you get to page 276 from the bottom of the page. Let me know when you have that, please.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: On page 276 the document, the Security Council document S/25479 begins and continues then on for some pages, and can you confirm for the Judges that what is set out as document -- UN document S/25479 is a set of the Vance-Owen proposals or plan as it existed on the 26th of March as signed by Izetbegovic and also agreed by Mate Boban?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Did you mean S/25479 or 76?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: 79, please. On page 2 -- on page 276 on the right side of the page.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ah, yes. I see it. Excuse me. Yes, that is the document. You note its date, dated 26 March 1993. That is one day after President Izetbegovic signed the complete Vance-Owen Plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Now, sir, because of the time I'm going to -- we're going to begin to press forward a bit harder because we're going to need to conclude before too much longer. Can I ask -- yes, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: The record speaks of a document number 03198.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. That's the exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: It's not 1398?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Ah-huh. But it says 003 and something. So one goes looking for something that one doesn't have. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honour. I was not -- frankly I'm not paying that much attention to the monitor I didn't see that, but you're absolutely right. That is the exhibit -- the proper Exhibit number for the record is P 01398.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sorry for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In that packet, starting at page 276, is the UN document, again for the record, S, as in Susan, /25479?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, can I ask you for the purposes that -- this afternoon, can I ask you to go to page 280, page 280, and section that is titled E withdrawal of forces.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is the text of the Vance-Owen Peace Plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And once again can you just read that section out loud, please.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It reads: "Sarajevo Province shall be immediately demilitarised. All Serb forces shall withdraw into Provinces 2, 4 and 6; HVO (Croatian Defence Council) forces into Province 3; Bosnian army forces into Province 1. Both Bosnian army and HVO forces shall be deployed in Provinces 5, 8, 9 and 10 under arrangements agreed between them. The process of demilitarisation shall apply to it all forces in all these nine provinces, and shall be carried out under the supervision of UNPROFOR and in accordance with the detailed arrangements and timetables in the Agreement for peace in Bosnia and Herzegovina, or as negotiated in the Mixed Military Working Group."

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And, sir, can you just simply confirm for us that that is indeed everything that the Vance-Owen Plan as of the end of March 1993 as agreed by Izetbegovic, is that everything it says about the withdrawal of forces in provinces 5, 8, 9 and 10?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is everything that the Vance-Owen Plan explicitly said, and it so remained through May. It was never changed thereafter.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Let me just ask you to briefly look at a joint statement which is marked as Exhibit P 01738. And --

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And can you just confirm for us that it was essentially a statement or a declaration made by President Izetbegovic and President Franjo Tudjman essentially confirming the agreement that we've been talking about in the last few minutes and extending their hopes, et cetera, in support for moving forward with the agreement?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, let's me turn -- ask you to look next to 1792, P 01792. And did you come to know, you and Secretary Vance and Lord Owen, come to know around this time that subsequent to the signature of the Vance-Owen Plan by President Izetbegovic or around the 26th, the 25th the 26th of March 1993 that the Bosnian Croats then proposed that a further statement be signed by President Izetbegovic?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were aware of that, and we were also aware that Izetbegovic never signed it. He did not agree with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And if I can ask you to look at the document which again is P 01792. Can you again confirm to us that as far as you know President Izetbegovic never signed this statement proposed by Mate Boban?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm certain he never signed it. Because in addition, extremely heavy fighting and ethnic cleansing by the HVO began in April.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In that connection, can I next ask you to go to P 01798. Sir, this is a record of an HVO meeting on the 3rd of April, 1993, and again I just want to point some passages to you and ask for your reaction to them. You will see as you turn to the -- if you go to page 2 of the minutes toward the bottom of that page there's a paragraph that stays: "Until the republic is fully demilitarised." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: At the end of that it says the statement was signed by Mr. Mate Boban and its integral text reads as follows," and then does it essentially and if you need if you'd like or if you've had a chance before to compare the text that set out in the minutes to the joint statement proposed by Mr. Boban that we were just looking at, Exhibit P 01792, did the minutes essentially set out that joint statement?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't compared them, but I would assume, and I think pretty safely, that it -- being -- it was a document, that it would quote the earlier Bosnian Croat document accurately, the one that Izetbegovic never signed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Very well. And there will be -- if anyone chooses to compare them in the courtroom there will be the opportunity to do so. Again, paragraph number 3 of both the joint statement that we looked at a moment ago, the proposed -- the proposed joint statement which was never joint, and paragraph number 3 on page 2 again talks about the armed forces of the ABiH in regions number 3, 8 and 10 being put under the control of the Main Staff of the HVO. Do you see that? Paragraph number 3.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: On page 2?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Page 3, if I misspoke.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, sorry. Yes, I see it. Paragraph 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And do you see again in both the joint statement and in the text of the minutes the date being -- the date being called for was 15 April 1993?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I can direct your attention further down the page. After item number 6: "The HVO HZ HB hopes that because of the enormous importance of the statement Mr. Alija Izetbegovic will sign this document because it is yet further evidence of a desire for peace, which everybody wants." And then finally the next two paragraph -- last paragraph on page 3 and the first paragraph on page 4. Perhaps you could read those two paragraphs for us?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The last two paragraphs?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, the last paragraph on the bottom of page 3 and the first paragraph on the top of page 4.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The last paragraph at the bottom of page 3 reads: "At this meeting, the HVO HZ HB adopted the position that if the aforementioned statement is not signed by the leaders of the Muslim delegations in provinces numbers 3, 8, and 10, then the basic premise in the peace plan which states that all ethnic armed forces have to withdraw to their domicile provinces should apply." The next paragraph reads: "If the joint statement is not implemented, the appropriate military and other authorities of the HVO HZ HB shall implement this provision of the Basic Document of the peace plan in regions number 3, 8, and 10. At the same time, the HVO HZ HB will respect the jurisdiction of the authorities in the provinces predominantly populated by the two other peoples." And before I ask you a couple of questions about that, can I ask you to first go to Exhibit P 09519. It should be at the back of the bundle you're in I'm told. P 09519.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, this is an article that was published in the newspaper Slobodna Dalmacija on the 4th of April, 1993, and I would just like you again to look at it long enough to see does this article essentially then set out basically the same information as was set out in the minutes of the HVO meeting and again encompassing in part the draft joint statement that Mr. Izetbegovic never signed?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, a quick perusal reveals that this is a description of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And the beginning of the article, just to put this in context says: "'Mostar at its session on Saturday the Croatian Defence Council of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna reviewed the documents of the peace plan which was signed by the representatives of the Croatian and the Muslim people in BH,' announced the press department of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna." So that was something like a press release, I take it, press statement?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, on this point, sir, can you just tell us again the course of action outlined in the HVO minutes, including the paragraph that you read out loud to us a couple of moments ago, did the Vance-Owen Peace Plan at any time contemplate unilateral efforts to enforce that plan without agreement?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Nothing like that was ever contemplated or written in the Vance-Owen Peace Plan. We have read appendix section E, which set forth the Vance-Owen Peace Plan very clearly, and there is nothing about the -- this kind of action in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And can you just tell the Judges briefly as we're coming to the final set of questions here, did you and Secretary Vance and Lord Owen, did you become aware around mid-April 1993, in fact, a major armed conflict then broke out between the Croats and Muslims in Central Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we did, and it was widely known throughout the world. The press covered it extensively. Television pictures were shown on CNN, BBC, particularly concerning the HVO depredations in Central Bosnia, and it reached the United Nations, which issued statements and -- condemning the Bosnian Croat action.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I can ask you to go to Exhibit P 01983. And this is a UN document, and can you just simply confirm that this records for UN purposes a statement that was made by President Izetbegovic and Mr. Boban on the 18th of April following the outbreak of that conflict?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This was the, I must say, typical protestations of peaceful intent signed by the parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Why do you say you must say typical protestations?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because we would see over and over again, particularly Mate Boban and the Bosnian Croats, declaring their fielty to Bosnia-Herzegovina, their love of peace, their willingness to live in multi-ethnic societies, but the action, of the HVO, the army on the ground, belied those statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Ambassador, could I ask you next please to go to P 02059.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: This is again a record of a meeting at President Tudjman's offices in Zagreb on the 24th of April, 1993. Again on the first page we have President Tudjman welcoming various people to the meeting, including a delegation -- well, delegations led by Lord Owen, Mr. Izetbegovic, and Mate Boban. And can I ask you to turn to page 11, please, of that transcript.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And starting at page 11, Izetbegovic after a comment by Franjo Tudjman, and then he essentially gives the floor to Mr. Izetbegovic and says and then -- and then Mr. Boban will have the floor. Alija Izetbegovic says: "Ladies and gentlemen, I agree with President Tudjman. This is obviously a political issue. For me it presents itself in the following way: Do Croatia, the Republic of Croatia and the Croatian Defence Council want the Vance-Owen Plan honestly and fully by the spirit and by the letter? I said by the spirit and by the letter. "My impression is that they do not. I'll explain why. As it is known we signed this plan with a lot of hesitations, reservations, and difficulties. It was very difficult for us to decide to put our sit on that plan."

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Your Honour, with great respect, this has absolutely no probative value whatsoever for Mr. Scott to be reading statements said to express the thoughts of Mr. Izetbegovic and is probably going to ask the witness to somehow confirm it. I don't think there's been any showing the witness was at this meeting and it's really completely improper.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, Ambassador, can you confirm your presence at this meeting with Mr. Vance and Mr. Owen?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think Mr. Vance was there, was he?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: He may not have been. My apology. He was referring -- I was looking at the reference to Mr. Vance and Mr. Owen. If you would like to check your diary?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would have to check my diary.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In light of the question that's been raised, please do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: My objection is far broader than that. It is to the witness being asked to listen while Mr. Scott reads what the -- the thoughts of Mr. Izetbegovic, as if they were evidence in this case and had some probative value.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well Your Honour, my intention was to do what I have done previously yesterday and today, and this is a man who knows the course of these negotiations, knows the Vance-Owen Plan I suspect certainly better than anyone in this room, and can give his views on whether it was properly being applied and implemented at this time or not as he has been doing throughout his testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The Trial Chamber will rule, but Mr. Praljak is on his feet.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd just like to remind you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, only if it concerns procedure.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This concerns procedure alone. When there was a protected witness, a High Representative of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna here and he was to be asked about refugees, and he was far more involved with the Croatian people than Ambassador is and he knew far more about other people's thoughts, then the Judges told me that I couldn't put such questions to the witness, that this was beyond the scope of the witness's knowledge from Vares. The subject matter we are dealing with here is far broader. No one is reacting, so I would like to inform of the fact that I feel confused by this since the accused and the Defence are not being treated in an identical manner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ambassador, in order for the Judges to be quite clear about the objection, the Prosecution has shown you this document, 2059. It concerns a meeting that was attended by Lord Owen, Mr. Tudjman, Mr. Izetbegovic, and Mr. Mate Boban. The meeting started at 2055 hours. Were you yourself present at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not recall, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm putting this question to you because the Prosecution, on page 11 of the minutes of this meeting, referred to what Mr. Izetbegovic said, and, if you were present, the Prosecutor can ask you whether what we can see on paper was actually said or not, but you have just told us you're not sure whether you were present at the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Could I ask the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Sorry, I have --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Judge Trechsel, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Yes, it's on. Mr. Okun, I have your diary in front of me. It is page, I think, 4543, and you account the whole day, and then there is 7.20 to 8.30 p.m., dinner with Tudjman and others, and then it does not go on. The next page is 9 -- oh, yes. Then it is 9.00 p.m. to 11.10 p.m. Croatia/BH meeting, and there you seem to have been present.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, in answer to your question, Judge Antonetti, and I apologise for not recalling directly whether I was present at this meeting in 1993, but I thank the Judge, I was present.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I believe it's in -- in e-court. If people care to, and it may not be necessity point, but if people care to in Exhibit -- which diary is this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Scott, the witness was there, so you may ask your questions because he may or may not remember. We, the Judges, don't know what he will say, but since he was there, you may continue and ask your questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I believe I left off approximately on page 12 at the second -- well, the third paragraph, I suppose, beginning on that page that says: "Our impression." I'm not sure exactly, to be honest, and the transcript has moved on, but let's start there. "Our impression is that the HVO and the Republic of Croatia do not want the Vance-Owen Plan as it stands. "First of all, we accepted this plan because we thought that Bosnia and Herzegovina could not contain some exclusively ethnic and national territories, because it is a mixed country. "Its basic problem is that it is an ethnically mixed country. "Judging by the HVO actions, they understood this plan in a completely different manner. Despite the fact that under the mediation of Mr. Vance and Mr. Owen, we have signed a document, an agreement, whose first item explicitly says that the provinces are not national territories of any one of the peoples, who cannot lay claim to it only for themselves. If we have signed this ... "The second item of our agreement says that the symbols of Bosnia and Herzegovina will be respected and will also be displayed in the Travnik and Mostar provinces. "In other words, Herceg-Bosna as a state entity, as a type of state entity, could not exist after the signing of the Vance-Owen Plan. "During talks with Mr. Owen, I heard several times that this was only a temporary solution until the problem in Bosnia-Herzegovina was solved, that Herceg-Bosna was a temporary solution until some other solution was found. In our opinion the Vance-Owen Plan offered a permanent solution. However, after that Herceg-Bosna began to assert itself even more and impose itself by force. The Mostar and Travnik provinces were called Croatian provinces. The conflict in Travnik began when one morning all of Travnik was decorated with Croatian flags. So we have nothing against the Croatian flag, but the flag of Bosnia and Herzegovina should also have been displayed. So by signing the Vance-Owen Plan as we thought" -- excuse me -- "we thought we had finally solved the issue of the equality of the Croatian and Muslim peoples in these provinces which are now under the control of the HVO and the Bosnian army. "Instead, throughout the territory of Herceg-Bosna, the Muslim people continued to be disempowered. We expected that power-sharing would be the first thing of the Vance-Owen Plan that would be implemented in accordance with the envisaged ratios. "When people from Herzegovina asked us what our motives were to sign the Vance-Owen Plan, we told them, please, this is a way for you to finally participate in government because for a long time the Muslim people, some people in Herzegovina, in Mostar, in some places around Travnik, had not participated in government. "The conflict erupted because only Croatian authority began to be implemented in the Mostar and Travnik provinces." Ambassador, I'm going to stop there. As I've asked you at other times this afternoon, again as an architect of the Vance-Owen Plan and what you observed and the interpretations and the implementation, the attempted implementation of this plan, what is your reaction to President Izetbegovic's comments?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I think at this point, Your Honour, I will object. First of all, there's no foundation as to what Izetbegovic is saying that this gentleman knows directly from being on the ground. The fact that he was present when this was said doesn't mean that it's absolutely so. In other words, he cannot offer this -- you know, this is hearsay, obviously, today. We don't have Mr. Izetbegovic. Had he been here or if he was here with us, we could cross-examine him. So it is a violation of our right of confrontation, number one. Number two, the gentleman does not know firsthand of these facts. The fact that he was told of these facts doesn't actually mean that these events as they're being described by Mr. Izetbegovic actually occurred as they're being described. I think the document speaks for itself. I think now to ask this gentleman whether he can vouch for, vouch for the authenticity and the reliability and the truthfulness for what Mr. Izetbegovic is saying is a bit of a stretch.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, my reaction is to that, number one, whether Mr. Izetbegovic is available or not is completely beside the point. It has -- has absolutely no bearing on this question at all. There are all sorts of documents and records that come in before the Chamber where the author or speaker is not before the Chamber. That has no significance whatsoever. Secondly, what I've asked the Ambassador to do as to those portions of what I've just read where Mr. Izetbegovic talks about the implementation of the Vance-Owen Plan, about power sharing, about mixed governments, about them not being national provinces, my question to him is whether that -- those statements, those characterisations of the Vance-Owen Plan are proper, and he -- no one more than Mr. -- Ambassador Okun can confirm that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: May I answer?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: May I -- may I just add a point? Maybe it would be helpful for the Defence if they looked at the journal, at the diary of the witness where in essence the text that Mr. Scott has read out finds an echo which -- which is, I think, at least prima facie evidence that the witness actually heard Mr. Izetbegovic, and he certainly has a view of whether what he heard there translates the spirit, the idea of the VOPP or not. It calls for his view on what he heard and noted. I do not understand why it should not be -- okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If -- if we're asking the gentleman to now opine on whether Mr. Izetbegovic, his understanding of the VOPP, is correct, then obviously as being one of the architects he can say yes or he can say no or whatever. If that is the narrow nature of if. If on the other hand he is being asked because there was a long list of reading that occurred, if he is asked to opine and authenticate and vouch for those events that's where I draw the line. Now, if the question was rephrase and narrowed, I don't have an objection and I concur with you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: So we are in harmony. This is a rare moment. Let's cherish it.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Trechsel. Indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir I think you know -- Ambassador I think you know the outstanding question. If you can answer that please?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can answer the question and I thank the Judge for calling attention to my journal entry which was contemporaneous. It was written as Izetbegovic was speaking on April 24th, 1993. This is what he said. It's in the diary. As the Judge said, it's echoed in the diary. That's point one. Point two is that the description of the plan given by President Izetbegovic is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Ambassador. Sir, I have one final exhibit for you to look at and then one or two final questions, and then we will be concluded with this part of your examination. Could I ask you to look at Exhibit P 02078. 2078.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] While --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] While this is being done, I don't know how the Prosecutor has not noticed this. In the joint statement, it says in the preamble of this document that the gentleman did attend this meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Do you have the exhibit, sir, 2078? Do you have the exhibit?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. And, sir, do you recall that around this time there were further -- after, again, the break -- the breakout of the -- of a major conflict when the Croats, the Muslims in Bosnia-Herzegovina in mid-April 1993, there were -- there was an additional meeting or series of meetings in Zagreb, and I think if you look at this page the people are listed including yourself on the top part. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hmm. I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Could you tell us briefly about that meeting, the outcome?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, Your Honours. We can't base our questions on the statement, there was a large conflict between Muslims and Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Where in Bosnia-Herzegovina? We don't know what area we are talking about. Was there a conflict between the HVO and anybody else at that particular point in time?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If Mr. Praljak would take the time to look at the text of the document itself, it's quite clear that President Tudjman and President Izetbegovic and the others knew what they were -- apparently knew what they were talking about when they talk about in paragraph 3 and following about the violations of humanitarian law and the crimes committed by all sides in Bosnia-Herzegovina in April 1993. So contrary to Mr. Praljak, apparently Mr. Tudjman and others knew what they were talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, can you tell us about this meeting that occurred on around the 24th of April, 1993?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would prefer to compare it with my diary entry of that date.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If you're able to do that, if you have it available. If you know which -- just a moment and I see if I can find it.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: My diary is 2.000 pages long. I don't have it at my fingertips.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I will try to assist you if you tell me which -- it's in e-court?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the Honourable Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I know. I pressed the button. Yes. Now it should work. It is the pages preceding 4545. It must be 45 --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: For the record, Exhibit P 01772. If we can go in e-court to page 60 of that document in e-court. I believe you'll have it and the Ambassador will be able to look at it either on the screen or if he has it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that General Petkovic wanted to intervene.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PETKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, thank you very much. I would like to remind everybody that the transcript that was read out to the witness was actually a conversation that was held on that evening in Zagreb and that the Ambassador attended it, and the conclusion does not arise from a different meeting. These conclusions arise from those conversations. The transcript was the conversation which took place in Zagreb. I attended it and the Ambassador did, and after that conversation a joint statement was issued. We're not talking about two different documents or two different meetings. We are talking about just one meeting and this is the statement that arises from that meeting which has a military annex that we signed. This meeting happened on the 24th in the evening, and we're not talking about two different meetings. The meeting took place on the 24th. The transcript says what was said at the meeting and the conclusion -- conclusions are summarised in the statement. I was there and the gentleman was there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much for this clarification.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Apparently there is no dispute about it and Mr. Petkovic has also authenticated the document, which the Prosecution appreciates, his assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So, sir, if you have your diary in front of you?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: On the screen. If you look on the screen we can pull up the relevant page and if you want to look at it for a moment. I don't know that it's apparently in dispute now that, once again, various of the accused have confirmed the existence and the statement issued as the result of the meeting?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember this meeting. It was a very emotional meeting. It was heated. It was understandably very argumentative meeting because the fighting was continuing and indeed was escalating between the HVO and government army, and you can see in my diary written at the time, and I noted the times, at 10- or 15-minute intervals, I note on the left in parentheses at one point Mr. Izetbegovic speaking excitedly, Mate Boban interrupting, Izetbegovic still it excited, accusingly, et cetera. It was a very, very disputatious meeting, and it was called, that is to say the purpose of it, the reason we wanted to bring Tudjman, President Tudjman, and Izetbegovic together was to see if it was possible in the presence of President Tudjman to end this escalating violence, because it wasn't enough that Mate Boban would give his agreement even if he kept it, because we needed in many of the matters concerning the Bosnian Croats, the person who was in charge was President Tudjman.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And was the statement that the joint statement that is marked as Exhibit P 02078, to your recollection, issued or publicised as a result at the conclusion of this meeting?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the exact degree to which it was publicized in the Muslim or Croatian press, but it was issued and it was not obeyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And finally sir on the Vance-Owen Peace Plan, signing -- perhaps was the peace plan ever fully agreed? Did the parties ever agree and was there ever any final agreement and implementation of the Vance-Owen Peace Plan?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We're now at the end of April. This was also a difficult period because the Bosnian Serbs were continuing their attacks at a much -- at a much reduced level, which is what allowed the HVO to start the ethnic cleansing again in Central Bosnia, but the Bosnian Serbs, Karadzic, Koljevic, Krajisnik, continued to be completely recalcitrant vis-a-vis the Vance-Owen Peace Plan. Lord Owen and I met just about this time, at the end of April, in Belgrade with President Milosevic who called Karadzic to come to the meeting. Karadzic was not there when it started, and the discussion of Milosevic and Karadzic and Lord Owen and myself concerned the effort, very strong effort on our part, to get Karadzic to agree. He was recalcitrant. He made various false statements, as was his want. Secretary Vance was then in New York attending to other business, and at one point during this meeting it was asked that we call Secretary Vance to get his view directly on a certain point that I had made, and we did so. We called Secretary Vance. He came on the line. He spoke to Milosevic and us and Karadzic, and he agreed with what I had said, but you can see the intensity of the meeting, of the effort to bring the Serbs on board by this fact. Well, Milosevic, incidentally, whether honestly or not, one never knew with Milosevic, was arguing in favour of Bosnian Serb adherence to the Vance-Owen Plan. In any case, the meeting ended in inconclusively. But a few days later the Greek Foreign Minister called us in Geneva and said he would like to convene a large meeting of foreign ministers, our group, others as well, in Athens to pressure Karadzic and the Bosnian Serbs to sign the Vance-Owen Peace Plan. That meeting took place on May 2, 1993. I was there, of course, and it was a long day, but Karadzic had already decided that he would sign with one condition. So Karadzic did sign all three parts of the Vance-Owen Peace Plan on May 2nd, 1993, in Athens in our presence. Champagne was handed out afterwards. A celebratory luncheon was held, but the delegates who were not involved, who had not dealt with Radovan Karadzic, did not pay much attention to the fact that his one condition on signing the Vance-Owen Peace Plan was that it had to be approved by the Bosnian Serb Assembly, that his approval was not final. And so two weeks later, the Bosnian Serb Assembly met and rejected the plan, and that was the end of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Ambassador, I want to thank you for coming to The Hague once again and giving your evidence. I want to thank you also for the service that you performed during this time in 1992 and 1993, and wish you a continued good stay here in The Hague. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ambassador, just a brief question from you as a result of the intervention by General Petkovic. In the last document, which is a joint statement, you were there. Your name appears on the document. As far as I could understand, the meeting started in the evening at 20.55. Then there were statements by the parties. We heard what President Izetbegovic said because the Prosecutor has read it out loud to us. It seems on the basis of this document that the -- the participants in the meeting had been given that text. There was a break at 23.10 for an hour, and then the meeting continued at 10 minutes after midnight, and the document was signed 45 minutes after the -- after midnight, and the meeting ended 10 minutes before 1.00, and as far as I could understand from General Petkovic, this document was the result of the meeting at which you had discussed the wording of this statement. Is that the fact? Is this what you remember about this meeting? According to the documents that we have before us, it seems as a result of the meeting that there was a joint stating by the three signatories, Mr. Boban, Mr. Izetbegovic, and it was signed in the presence of President Tudjman, who was there as a witness. In reality, this is a joint statement by Mr. Boban and Mr. Izetbegovic in the presence of President Tudjman. Is this how you remember this meeting to have taken place? Is this, what I have just said, a good reflection of the course of the meeting?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, it is. The statement, and you correctly pointed out the break in the meeting, the statement was not drafted or co-drafted by us. It was essentially President Tudjman's chair, the meeting of Boban and Izetbegovic, and it was the three of those gentlemen who developed the statement, and it was precisely in that break period that you alluded to. So General Petkovic is correct. This is what emerged from the meeting of Boban, Izetbegovic, with President Tudjman, and there was a -- that was the small meeting within the larger meeting, as you surmised.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: As we are speak -- as we are speaking about this, may I refer to your diary page 4548. That is the final page on the text and perhaps it can be put on the e-court. It's just actually three pages down. There you -- you also write down these moments in time.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, I don't have that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: No, it's coming up.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: On the left side. And you see now on this break you comment a drafting exercise, useless. Did you write that before the next entry or would you like to comment on this?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we were at the same table, so there was drafting with us, but it was -- with us at the table it didn't work. It -- they got a statement of the -- of the three, because you see afterwards at midnight, and the arguing is continuing, but at the same time they -- President Tudjman got them to agree to a statement. At this point, as Judge Antonetti pointed out, it was close to 1.00 a.m. in the morning, and people were -- were ready to sign a statement to go home.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: If I understand you correctly, at 11 -- at 12.15 you were still of the opinion that this would never work out, and then, after all, somehow it did.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: President Tudjman was a very persuasive man.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, I would like to go back to the place and the role played by President Tudjman in these negotiations. In the transcript of this meeting that took place on the 25th of April, he signed as a witness to this agreement between Mr. Boban and President Izetbegovic. Yesterday, you told us that he was not the head of the Croatian delegation of the Croats from Bosnia. Today in the transcript, on page 68, line 15, you have told us that President Tudjman was in charge of the Bosnian Croats and all the while you were answering President Antonetti's question you kept repeating that he chaired that meeting. My question to you is this: You attended that meeting. Would you say that during those negotiations and during this conflict the effective role of President Tudjman had somehow evolved and turned into something else? What was his role? What was his position?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: President Tudjman was president of the Republic of Croatia, a recognised state, a member of the United Nations, a man with whom we had close relations, Secretary Vance and I, because we had worked closely with him already in 1991 during the Serb attack on Croatia. At the same time, he was the dominant figure as far as the Bosnian Croats were concerned. He had no formal title in Bosnia-Herzegovina, but there was no doubt who gave the orders to Mate Boban. You may recall at a meeting we discussed yesterday, Judge, President Tudjman at one point says, and Boban is sitting there, I think, about the extension of the term by Alija Izetbegovic as president, remember in December 1992 he was supposed to turn over the Presidency on a rotational basis to a Bosnian Croat member of the Bosnian Presidency, and President Tudjman says, "Well, you know, Boban objected," words to that effect, "they should have done it, but I told Boban it was okay." "I recommended to Boban," I believe, was his word, and it was okay. And of course Boban agreed. So it wasn't just a question of whether President Tudjman needed or had any formal position in the Bosnian governmental structure. He did not. But as the president of Croatia, he was the ruler of the Bosnian Croats. Have I answered your question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's 5.30, and we'll now have our 20-minute break. We'll then start with the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll now resume, and I will give the floor to the Defence team that will be starting first.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President. Good afternoon, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Ambassador. We haven't formally met. My name is Michael Karnavas, and I'm an attorney from the United States. With my co-counsel here, Suzana Tomanovic, we represent Dr. Jadranko Prlic. Now, you've indicated to us today -- I'm going to pick up from where you left off, you said you had close relations with Dr. Tudjman; correct?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And I take it that was because at least initially when Mr. Vance got involved, I believe that you were with him, that was in order to solve the situation in Croatia because Croatia had been attacked by the JNA.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We began in October 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And yesterday and today you made a point of telling us in no uncertain terms that it was Dr. Tudjman that actually was the head of the Bosnian Croats. If not an official title, but basically he was the godfather. He did everything, gave the orders, and everybody obeyed pretty much. That's what you told us, right?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was the de facto head. I would not say that he was responsible for every jot and tittle of Bosnian Croat behaviour. No leader is. But he was the final word on the major decisions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, I mention that because at least one question that's begged to be answered is: Why bother with Mate Boban? Why bother with any Croat from Bosnia? Why not just go straight to Tudjman? You had these close relations. He gave the orders. He could snap his fingers and make things done. He could sign. Why just -- why not just cut the middleman out and go directly with Mr. Tudjman?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's not the way the world works. Mr. Boban had a title. Mile Akmadzic was the Prime Minister of the country. Bosnia and Herzegovina was a recognised sovereign, independent country within internationally recognised borders, and so we dealt with the recognised authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. But you could recognise -- you could deal with the recognised authorities openly, but you could have had a sort of a two-track approach. Openly embrace Mate Boban and privately just deal with Tudjman and have him -- and cut your deal with Tudjman. Why not do it that way? If -- if assuming that you are correct that Tudjman was the alpha and omega for the Croats both in Croatia and for the Croats in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the reason quite simply is that's not the way Secretary Vance and I work. We don't do something in public and something else privately.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, you've testified three times before in this Tribunal, and frankly I've looked at all of these -- these transcripts very carefully, and you weren't asked the question directly, but obviously you were talking about the events in Bosnia-Herzegovina. At no time -- at no time did you say in your testimony that it was Tudjman that actually was calling all the shots the way you emphasised it today and yesterday.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's a very simple reason for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You would agree with me that you never mentioned --

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't agree with that, but I'm going to answer your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Go for it.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The three times that I testified before, I was testifying always against Serbs. In one case, President Milosevic. The other case was Mr. Krajisnik, the Bosnian Serb number two. And the other case were the JNA officers responsible for the atrocity at Vukovar. So the focus was exclusively, almost exclusively on Serb and Bosnian Serb activity. It would have been extraneous to drag President Tudjman into it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, in the Krajisnik case, as I understand, one of the reasons Krajisnik was indicted and was convicted and was involved in this whole picture of Bosnia-Herzegovina had to do with his involvement in -- in the government, in the RS government at the time, or the pseudo-government I believe as you pointed out -- put it yesterday, and at least in part the questions that were being posed to you by the Prosecution and by the Defence dealt with negotiations, right?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Negotiations can whom?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: With Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: To a degree. Krajisnik was generally not present at our negotiations, and that came out if you recheck the transcript. I was asked that question and, of course, it was confirmed in my diary that we saw Karadzic, Dr. Karadzic, and Koljevic, both of whom speak good English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Much more frequently than we saw Mr. Krajisnik, who tended to remain more as, so to speak, the inside Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. But the -- I guess my line of questioning is that with -- the context in which you testified it in the Krajisnik case had to do with peace negotiations, whether it was -- whether it was Krajisnik or Karadzic, you were being asked questions about the various parties.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And we saw yesterday and today you touched a little bit on the Serbs. You told us a little bit about Milosevic. You told us about Karadzic. And just by curiosity when I look at your testimony, there's nothing about you claiming that Tudjman was in fact representing the Croats. I'm just making that observation. Okay? Would you agree with me at least if we went through --

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: If that's the case --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- that means I was not asked the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I answer the questions --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- counsel, that are asked to me. I don't go off on -- I hope I don't go off on excursions to waste the Court's time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, I looked at your -- at your diary as well, and I didn't see any notations in your diary you make comments, because in your diary you make comments based on meetings, based on observations. There's nothing in your diary where you say that Tudjman is in fact the representative of the Croat people for -- in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Would you agree with me that there's nothing in the 2.000 pages of diaries where you come out and say that?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I do not agree with you at all, and indeed the diaries -- you have misdescribed the diaries.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because -- if I may continue?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We've mentioned this before, a very important meeting with President Tudjman, Mate Boban there where they discussed a very important question which we've discussed before, but you've asked so I must answer, concerning the continuation in the Presidency after December 1992 of Izetbegovic when the Presidency should have rotated to a Bosnian Croat and President Tudjman says, "I recommended," which I put in quotes in the diary you'll recall, I hope.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I recall that.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: And that's perfectly evident. We all smiled when he said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everybody knew what that meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: "Everybody knew what that meant." Huh. Well, I don't see it in your diary what everybody knew what that meant.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let me continue then.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Hold on, hold on. Let me -- first of all, it's not in your diary; second of all, you -- right now we don't have Tudjman over here to tell us anything, but you're interpreting a smile or a word, recommend, as if he was the one that was able to order Boban. Now, why wouldn't he say if he was that powerful as you -- as you claim he is, why didn't he just say, I ordered Boban to do it?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because he's a courteous gentleman.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: And it's in my diary and he continued to say, and it's -- you can read the diary entry. He continued to say and he did it, you know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well yesterday I recall you saying I'm moving fast and I apologise for asking rapid questions because it's only -- I need four days with you, to be honest, and we don't have that time. But I'll slow down a little bit for the interpreters. But yesterday you indicated that occasionally Boban would say, Well, I need to clear it up with -- check with Tudjman. At least you made one reference at least at one time Boban said that he had to get clearance or he had to check it Tudjman. Do you recall saying that yesterday? In other words, that it was so obvious that Boban was getting his marching orders from Tudjman that when he was being asked, his response occasionally, or at least on an important issues would be I have to -- I have to talk to Tudjman.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that -- that was Boban's attitude.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, again maybe I'm a stickler for precision, but I don't see anything in your diary that reflects that.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm just asking you a question, is it in there or not?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm really surprised at these questions --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Don't be.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- because we've spent several hours here going over meetings in Zagreb with President Tudjman in the chair. We have the pentagonal meetings in Geneva with President Tudjman there, and President Tudjman was indeed the man that had to be consulted. The last word was his.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now, as I said, and I try to say it again briefly, of course he was not consulted on every individual point because he had a country to run, namely Croatia, which was still being occupied by the Yugoslav army. So he did not spend as much time, you know, full time on -- on the Bosnian case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, I put to you, sir, that that's an incorrect observation on your part, and perhaps he was being consulted because, yes, he was an influential leader, but also at times, and I think we're going to we might get a chance to see it, if not through you, through other witnesses, that the internationals sought his assistance and he was acting as an interlocutor if you may -- if you may call it that, a more intermediary trying to cobble up or get the two parties to agree, at least the two parties, Izetbegovic and Boban. So I take -- I take exception to your characterisation. What do you have to say about that?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Simply you're incorrect.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: You've drawn an incorrect inference.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I should also call to your attention that the regular Croatian army was also in Bosnia-Herzegovina. There was no dispute about that. So that President Tudjman, who is a professional military man, a very distinguished general, a partisan fighter with the Partisans during World War II took a -- as you might expect took an interest in the activities of his own army.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, sir, was Croatia hosting any refugees from Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, a large number.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: By any chance, were any of those Muslim?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Was aid going from Croatia to the Muslims in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me. Allow me to answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. You can go with a yes and or no and then explain if you want.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The assistance that went through Croatia, I stress the word, "through," was very important for the Bosnian Muslims because, as we all know, Bosnia-Herzegovina is entirely surrounded by Serbia, then called Yugoslavia, and by the Republic of Croatia. So in order to get to the Muslims, one had to either go through those countries or overfly them, and indeed a great deal of aid id go to the Bosnian Muslim particularly, most of it supplied by Arab countries from the Gulf through Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. So -- so what you're telling us is if Croatia wanted to they could have closed the borders, not allow any aid to go to the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Not allow any weapons to go to the Muslims and, of course, not allow any refugees, any Muslim refugees to come from Bosnia to Croatia. Had -- I mean, if that had been --

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In theory they could have done that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The international community, however, would have been outraged and taken action if they did that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. You mean they would have been outraged if they had prevented weapons to be shipped to the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina so that it could then be used, turned around and be used to kill Croats? That would have been outrage about that?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, the outrage would be of course denying domicile, temporary domicile to the refugees. Croatia was a signatory to the refugee convention, and so they had an international legal obligation to take in the refugees. That's point one. And the second point was that the Croatian government did stop occasionally shipments aimed -- designed to go to the Bosnian government. I recall very well one time --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going to have to cut you off here. You've made your point we have to move on here I don't mean to be rude. It's just I have very limited time.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Fine. I understand. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That's all right.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: There was an embargo as far as arms were concerned, was there not?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. But that embargo wasn't really being observed?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not observed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yeah. In countries such as the United States, for instance, they might have had a two-track policy, openly saying we want the embargo but then turning a blind eye and we saw that for -- Galbraith was over here, John -- the Galbraith's son was here. He was the ambassador to Croatia at the time, Peter Galbraith. He was here and he told us that at one point Tudjman was approached by the Iranians to have weapons shipped through Croatia. He went to the Americans and they basically said we won't, you know, don't -- we won't object or we won't do anything about it. So that embargo was not being observed by the Americans as well.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: By some elements of the Americans.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Now, yesterday again I'm just hitting spots to, you know, just major points today and tomorrow maybe we'll slow down and go through some of your diary, but the Karadjordjevo thing, it's interesting. I looked at your -- I looked at your diary. I didn't see anywhere where you or Mr. Cyrus Vance ever mentioned anything about Karadjordjevo to Tudjman directly, or to Milosevic for that matter, to say hey, what is this agreement about? Why do you want to carve up Bosnia-Herzegovina? Or was that out of politeness that you chose not to confront him?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, first of all, the Karadjordjevo meeting occurred itself before we were involved. So did the Cvetkovic-Macek Agreement of August 1939 occur before we were involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: The answer is, it's not in there.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: But.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: It's not in your notebooks.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: But -- but on many occasions we raised the -- the problems involved with carving up Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Sir, I'm asking you concretely. Is there anywhere in your 2.000-page diary where you make a notation where Cyrus Vance, who was there on behalf of the United Nations, along with you, or -- or David Lord Owen who is there on behalf of the EU, is there anywhere in your diary where you confront Tudjman and say, What about this Karadjordjevo? Or you confront Milosevic? Or you confront both of them when they're together? Is there any inkling in that diary of yours?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would have to consult the diary.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: What if I were to tell you that I read all of your diary, not once but twice, and it's a long one, and there's no mention in there?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if you say it, I hear you saying it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And there's nothing, incidentally, about Graz either. One would think that you negotiators would talk to the man, Mr. Tudjman, who, you know, you've designated him as being the most powerful Croat. With your close relations, did you ever contact him directly to ask him what is this Graz agreement about and for him to put a stop with Mate Boban and Karadzic? Because I don't see anything in your notebook, by the way, in your notes reflecting that.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't want to go on at length, but the way negotiators work is to deal with the parties, to derive their positions from what they tell you or the documents they give you. You know, it's not a research operation or blah, blah unless we need important information --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Fair enough.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- because we were dealing directly with the issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, on this Karadjordjevo thing, yesterday you indicated that this was widely publicised or this was publicised.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was in the press.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: It was in the press. And -- but this was before your time, before Mr. Vance's time, but you yourself or Mr. Vance and Mr. Owen or anybody else in your -- in your entourage never met with anybody who actually witnessed this Karadjordjevo meeting. I mean, other than Milosevic and Karadzic and Tudjman, and we know that you -- they weren't spoken to about this.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they were the principals at this meeting, and we were dealing with them on a regular basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I understand. But --

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: So we didn't need to ask -- to take their attendance like schoolchildren, were you present at class that day?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I know but --

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because we were talking to them, Mr. -- counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: My question is this though I mean everybody seems to know what happened in Karadjordjevo. They all seem to know the content, the agreement, but nobody was there?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And nobody bothered to ask the two folks that supposedly made this agreement like, Hey, what's this agreement about. And my question is: Did you or anybody else ever meet anybody who was present that could at least tell us this was what was agreed upon at Karadjordjevo, other than what we read in the press?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, interesting and I take it -- sticking with this issue, I noticed that you were questioned once about Mr. Zimmermann who was the ambassador, the last ambassador to the -- to Yugoslavia; right?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And this has to do with the '92 agreement, I believe it was March, was it, March 18th, that -- that Izetbegovic signed and then he withdrew his sit. This is the Cutileiro Plan.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You recall that. And of course that's undisputed that he signed or -- and then he withdrew his signature, but there was some publications, it was widely publicised that it was Warren Zimmermann, none other than the American Ambassador, who actually had talked Izetbegovic -- or had talked him into withdrawing his signature. Do you recall that little exchange? In fact you say that was in the press, but it's unverifiable.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not only is it unverifiable, it was formally denied by Ambassador Zimmermann.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: When you had a conversation with him.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he wrote a book.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: You may read it in his book.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, I mean --

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he wrote the book. There's a document. You can read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, unfortunately he's not with us. But, of course, a wink is as good as a nod. He could have said, for instance, I don't think it's a good idea for you to go along with this. I'm not suggesting that's the case, but what I am suggesting here, what I am suggesting, the point I want to make is that we really can't always trust what we read in the press. Okay? That's the point that I'm trying to make because we can't cherry pick and say, Well, we just read in the press about Karadjordjevo. No proof what actually transpired, but here with Zimmermann, because we know him, we love him, he's one of us, obviously we must -- we must accept that. Graz. Let me go with Graz. Did you ever, sir, see a signed agreement, I mean with Boban's signature, agreeing to this Graz agreement? Yes, no, I don't recall.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Would it surprise you, sir, that Boban also publicly denied the Graz agreement?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wouldn't surprise me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And we'd have to take Boban's word for it.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Now, a couple of things. And I apologise for the rapid clip, you know. We're under a lot of pressure here with the time. And I don't mean to cut you off or be disrespectful. I don't want you to walk away thinking the Defence is disrespectful.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand. You're very fair.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, you gave a statement not too long ago before coming here. I believe it was this young lady that came to New York to see you or Washington, one of the two places. New York. And there in your statement, paragraph 5, you say and I'm just going to read part of it, it's not -- nothing --

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I have it with me. May I look at it?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You may. You may. It's paragraph 5. Paragraph 5. You can read along. It's just a short piece.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't believe I have this in e-court. I don't know if Your Honours have it, if the Prosecutor provided it to you. If it wasn't, I apologise. I could probably put this on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, read it out. We have trust in you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Paragraph 5 it says: "During this period the war aims, the war aims, policies and military activities of the three sides were, in the main, consistently applied. The war aims of the Bosnian Muslim government were: The creation of a unitary, centralised state of all its citizens, in the knowledge that such a state would have a Muslim plurality and with the expectation that this plurality would become a majority as the Muslim birth rate was considerably higher than that of the Croats and Serbs." That was your statement. You're shaking your head. Does that mean yes?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm agreeing with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: You have read it accurately.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you. I get a little nervous when I'm up here because my reading isn't as good as it should be. Now -- good. It seems here that you're telling us slightly more than what you told us yesterday, perhaps because you weren't asked, but here you're telling us not only is this a unitary, in other words, one person, one vote, but the ultimate goal of the Muslims which were a constituent element of Bosnia-Herzegovina, was eventually to be able to have a majority, and if you have a one person one vote, they rule over the other two constituent peoples.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not necessarily.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Not necessarily, but that could also -- but you can't exclude that possibility either?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would be a possibility. It would be a distant possibility because it would assume that hundreds of thousands of people would all vote in unison.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: And that rarely happens.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I understand that. But if you are a 17.2 or 3 per cent of the population, obviously this unitary approach to a government --
